query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability at 700–1000 °C is governed primarily by Al-driven chemical short-range order (CSRO): when the average number of Al–(Ni,Co) nearest-neighbour bonds per atom remains below a critical value of ≈0.35, the alloy retains a single FCC matrix with nanoscale CSRO clusters, whereas exceeding this threshold triggers long-range B2 ordering and macroscopic FCC + B2 phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted equiatomic CoCrFeNi ingot homogenised at 1200 °C/24 h, water-quenched; grain size ≈50 µm; single-phase FCC.
generation.intervention: Substitute Al for Ni in 1-at.% steps (0–10 at.% Al), followed by annealing at 900 °C for 24 h and water quench.
generation.conditions: Annealing in high-vacuum; 900 ± 5 °C; 24 h; water quench to room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Extent of Al-(Ni,Co) CSRO quantified by diffuse-scattering intensity around FCC {100} superlattice positions and by nearest-neighbour statistics from atom-probe tomography.
generation.mechanism: Negative mixing enthalpies (ΔH_mix < −15 kJ mol⁻¹) between Al and late transition metals favor local Al-rich clusters. As long as the CSRO clusters remain below the percolation limit (~0.35 Al–TM bonds/atom) they impede dislocation motion and delay diffusion without providing sufficient driving force for a first-order order–disorder transition. Beyond this limit, cooperative ordering lowers Gibbs free energy more than configurational entropy can compensate, nucleating B2 domains that coarsen with time.
generation.predicted_outcome: Al additions ≤4 at.%: (i) single FCC lattice, (ii) diffuse-scattering intensity increases by up to 300 % over baseline, (iii) room-temperature yield strength rises by ~150 MPa and the 800 °C yield strength rises by ~50 MPa relative to Al-free CoCrFeNi. Al ≥5 at.%: appearance of B2 superlattice peaks in XRD (>5 % volume fraction) and APT-visible B2 regions ≥5 nm; concomitant drop in ductility (>30 % reduction in total elongation).
generation.baseline: 0 at.% Al (CoCrFeNi) after the same 900 °C/24 h treatment: single FCC, no superlattice diffuse scattering, yield strength 240 MPa at 25 °C, 120 MPa at 800 °C.
generation.boundary: Valid for 700–1000 °C anneals shorter than 48 h and total Al content ≤10 at.%. Outside this window sluggish diffusion or additional intermetallics (e.g., σ phase) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Exact critical Al–TM bond fraction (0.35 ± 0.05) and associated strength increment may vary with grain size, impurities, or cooling rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloy series with 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 at.% Al replacing Ni. Subject each to 900 °C/24 h anneal and water quench. Characterise by (1) synchrotron XRD for diffuse and superlattice scattering, (2) atom-probe tomography to count Al–TM nearest neighbours, (3) compression tests at 25 °C and 800 °C.
measurements: Volume fraction of B2 phase from Rietveld refinement
Yield strength and total elongation at 25 °C and 800 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If an alloy with Al content ≤4 at.% exhibits a B2 volume fraction >2 % or if an alloy with ≥6 at.% Al remains single FCC with no superlattice peaks (<2 % B2) despite exceeding the critical Al–TM bond fraction, the hypothesis is falsified.
